summary: KS3 learners formalise probability as a measure on a bounded 0-to-1 line: 0 = impossible, 1/2 = even chance, 1 = certain, with the same point expressible as fraction, decimal or percentage and read fluently in both directions (event → position, position → event). The distinctive demand is separating fair/equally-likely devices (where P = favourable/total can be calculated by symmetry) from biased ones (loaded spinner, bent coin, drawing pin) where symmetry no longer gives the value — it is either stated/given or, where neither symmetry nor a stated value is available, estimated from repeated data — and refusing the equiprobability shortcut 'n outcomes, so 1/n each' unless the sections/outcomes are genuinely equal. Learners also re-anchor the bounds: no probability is below 0 or above 1, and a probability is never a raw count of outcomes.
misconceptions: Equiprobability bias — assuming n possible outcomes means each has probability 1/n even when they are not equally likely (biased spinner)
Believing a probability can exceed 1 or be stated as a raw count of outcomes
Comparing probabilities written in different notations by their surface digits without converting
Assuming every probability can be CALCULATED from symmetry, with no notion that some must be estimated from data

activities.title: Placing probabilities on the 0-to-1 measure line
steps: Work with a 0-to-1 line marked with the fixed landmarks 0 (impossible), 1/2 (even chance) and 1 (certain).
Place a probability of 0.7 and a probability of 1/4 at their correct positions, and read off the same point shown three ways as a fraction, a decimal and a percentage.
For each placement, state which landmark the event sits near and justify its position ('0.7 is above even chance, so toward the certain end').
Place a set of everyday-event cards on the scale and justify each position in words.
Test the bounds: try to place a marker beyond the certain end or below the impossible end and state why no probability can go there.
activities.insight: A probability is one point on a bounded measure line; the same value can be written as a fraction, decimal or percentage, and nothing can lie below 0 or above 1.

activities.title: Fair vs biased: when symmetry works and when it doesn't
steps: Start with a fair 3-section spinner (equal sections) and calculate each colour's probability as favourable/total — here the three colours genuinely sit at equal thirds; similarly a fair six-sided die gives each number a probability of 1/6 by symmetry.
Switch to a biased spinner that is STATED to be designed so red comes up 70% of the time, with the red section much larger. Predict where the three colours sit on the line BEFORE checking.

Use the stated 70% to place red, and run or observe repeated spins to see that the three colours do not come out at equal thirds — red's observed proportion tends to sit near 0.7, above even chance and toward the certain end, while blue and yellow together share roughly the remaining 0.3 (they may be close to each other, since their split is not given); a finite run only approximates each value rather than landing on it exactly.

Place P(red) = 0.7 above even chance, toward the certain end, and work out P(not red) = P(blue or yellow) = 0.3 by subtracting from 1, placing it below even chance (blue and yellow share that 0.3, and the split between them is not given).
State in words why 'three colours' did not guarantee '1/3 each' — only equal sections would.
Then consider a plain drawing pin, whose point-up probability is neither given by symmetry nor stated: decide that it can only be estimated from data, and explain why there is no symmetry to use.
activities.insight: Equal probabilities require equal sections/outcomes. For a biased device symmetry no longer gives the value: if the bias is stated you use the given value (red = 0.7); where neither symmetry nor a stated value is available (a drawing pin), the probability can only be estimated from repeated data. The scale applies in every case.

activities.title: Predict-observe-explain with a real drawing pin
steps: Before any testing, predict the probability that a dropped drawing pin lands point-up, and write down the number AND the reasoning.
Drop the pin 40–50 times, recording point-up and point-down tallies.

Compare the observed proportion to the prediction and note whether point-up and point-down came out roughly equal or clearly different; whatever the tallies show, explain why the pin's lack of symmetry means a value of 1/2 cannot simply be assumed.
Mark the estimated point-up probability on the 0-to-1 line at the position the data settle toward.
Explain what the stated-beforehand prediction revealed about the equiprobability assumption, and why this probability had to be estimated rather than calculated.
activities.insight: Stating a prediction and reason before testing exposes the 'two ways to land, so even chance' assumption; because the pin is asymmetric and no value is stated, its probability must be estimated from experiment rather than assumed to be a half, and the recorded data give that estimate.

activities.title: Ordering and converting mixed-notation probabilities
steps: Order a mixed set such as 40%, 1/4 and 0.3 from least to most likely by first converting all to a common form.
Convert each probability to a decimal (or a position on the line) and check: 1/4 = 0.25, which sits below 0.3, which sits below 40% = 0.4.
Decide whether each of several statements is possible — e.g. 'a probability of 6' or 'a probability bigger than 1' — and justify using the bounds.
Judge a fair-vs-biased claim: 'there are three colours, so each has probability 1/3' — decide whether it is right and explain when it would and would not hold.
activities.insight: Probabilities written in different notations must be converted to a common form before comparison; values cannot exceed 1 or be raw counts; '1/n each' holds only for genuinely equal sections/outcomes.

activities.title: Socratic challenges to the bounds and the 1/n shortcut
steps: Respond to a prompt such as 'Could a probability be 2?' and justify the answer using the 0–1 bounds.
Respond to 'Why isn't each colour 1/3 on this biased spinner?' and explain what would have to be true for 1/3 each to hold.
Explain how you would find P(not red) from P(red), and where it sits relative to even chance.
activities.insight: Articulating why values cannot exceed 1 and why '1/n each' needs equal sections consolidates the two central KS3 ideas in the learner's own words.

checkQuestion: Show a biased spinner with red, blue and yellow sections, and state that it is designed so red comes up 70% of the time. Ask the child to place P(red), P(blue or yellow), and describe P(not red) on a 0-to-1 scale. Then a classmate says 'there are three colours, so each has probability 1/3'. Ask: is that right, and why? Take the answer, then ask for the full reasoning (Tier 2).
checkAnswer: P(red) = 0.7, placed near the certain end; P(not red) = P(blue or yellow) = 0.3, below even chance; blue and yellow share the 0.3 between them. The classmate is wrong: 1/3 each would only hold if the three sections were equal, but this spinner is biased toward red — the number of colours does not fix the probabilities.
